problem: The attraction term is written a/[T0.5V(V + b)]. Read as printed, 'T0.5' means T × 0.5, so the student divides by half the temperature instead of the square root of the temperature. The value then differs by a factor of 2 and the RK term is wrong.
fix: Write the RK attraction term as a/(√T · V(V + b)), i.e. a divided by (square root of T) times V times (V + b). Similarly make clear that a in RK carries a T<sup>0.5</sup> in its units.

problem: Molar volume is quoted as 'V = 1 L', but V here is molar volume; the unit must be L/mol. The same slip appears in the aria description ('at 1 L'). The data points themselves are at 1 L/mol.
fix: Say 'At V = 1 L/mol the pressures are 24.94 bar and 22.41 bar.' and update the aria text to 'at 1 L/mol'. Also label the marker 'at V = 1 L/mol'.

problem: '(∂P/∂V) at Tc = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²) at Tc = 0' can be misread as differentiating with respect to Tc, or as conditions holding anywhere on the Tc isotherm. Both derivatives are zero only at one point: T = Tc, P = Pc, V = Vc.
fix: Write: at the critical point, (∂P/∂V)<sub>T=Tc</sub> = 0 and (∂²P/∂V²)<sub>T=Tc</sub> = 0, both evaluated at V = Vc and P = Pc.

problem: The answer says the gas is 'dense' and 'near saturation' at 0.5 L/mol. With the chapter's own numbers the van der Waals pressure there is about 40 bar, giving Z = PV/RT ≈ 0.80: a moderately non-ideal superheated vapour, not a near-saturated dense fluid. The stated reason overstates the case.
fix: Say: at 0.5 L/mol the compressibility factor is already about 0.8, so the departure from ideality is large and the two-term van der Waals model is too crude. Keep the advice to use a better cubic or a generalized correlation, and drop the 'near saturation' wording.

problem: Every symbol in the van der Waals formula is given with units except R ('R is the gas constant'), although the trap list later depends on knowing which R matches which units.
fix: Define R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (with V in m³/mol and P in Pa) or R = 0.08314 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (with V in L/mol and P in bar).
